title: Title, epigraphs and composition
short: Begun 27 March 1802 (stanzas 1-4), finished in 1804; printed in 1807 simply as 'Ode', and retitled in 1815.
body: Dorothy Wordsworth's journal for 27 March 1802 records that William wrote part of an ode; he reached the question that closes stanza 4 and then stopped, finishing stanzas 5-11 in early 1804. In Poems, in Two Volumes (1807) it closed the second volume under the title 'Ode' with the epigraph 'Paulo majora canamus' ('let us sing of somewhat greater things', Virgil, Eclogue 4.1), marking a rise in style. From 1815 it was called 'Ode: Intimations of Immortality from Recollections of Early Childhood', with an epigraph from 'My heart leaps up': 'The Child is Father of the Man'. The archive's text is the 1807 version (note the four lines on the grave in stanza 8, later cut).

title: Form: the irregular (Pindaric) ode
short: Stanzas of unequal length with lines from two to six stresses and irregular rhyme, in the 'Pindaric' manner of Cowley and Gray.
body: The English irregular ode, developed by Abraham Cowley from a misunderstanding of Pindar's metrics, allowed long and short lines to vary with the feeling. Wordsworth's line lengths swing from the dimeter 'To me did seem' to alexandrines such as 'The things which I have seen I now can see no more'. The eleven stanzas fall into three movements (1-4, 5-8, 9-11): loss, explanation, and consolation. The variety suits a poem that moves between lament, myth and argument.

title: Apparell'd in celestial light
short: Ordinary things seemed clothed in a heavenly radiance: the first statement of the 'glory' the poem mourns.
body: 'Apparelled' (clothed, dressed) makes light into a garment laid over things, so that the radiance appears to be added to them rather than seen in them. The poem's question is where that radiance came from: from the things, from the child's eye, or from a heavenly origin. Coleridge's 'Dejection', written in reply to these opening stanzas in April 1802, answers that the 'glory' comes from the soul itself.

title: The glory and the freshness of a dream
short: 'Glory' is the poem's key word, repeated in stanzas 1, 2, 4, 5 and 10; here it is likened to a dream.
body: The comparison to a dream is double-edged: it conveys vividness and also unreality. Cleanth Brooks's reading of the ode in The Well Wrought Urn (1947) stressed its paradoxes, and 'glory' and light do shift sense across the poem. The word recurs as 'a glory from the earth' (st. 2), 'the glory and the dream' (st. 4), 'clouds of glory' (st. 5) and 'glory in the flower' (st. 10).

title: The Rainbow comes and goes
short: The rainbow links the ode to 'My heart leaps up', written the day before (26 March 1802).
body: In 'My heart leaps up' the sight of the rainbow still moves the adult as it moved the child, and he hopes his days may be 'bound each to each by natural piety'. The ode, begun the next day, admits that the rainbow is still lovely but that something has gone from the seeing. Behind both lies the rainbow as God's covenant sign in Genesis 9:13. The 1815 epigraph made the connection explicit.

title: A timely utterance gave that thought relief
short: A famous crux: what was the utterance? Candidates include 'My heart leaps up', 'Resolution and Independence', or simply the act of speaking.
body: Wordsworth never identified it. Many editors suggest 'My heart leaps up' (26 March 1802), written the day before the ode was begun; others have proposed 'Resolution and Independence' (May 1802) or some other poem; still others read the phrase generally, as any expression that relieved the grief, perhaps this poem itself. The uncertainty matters because the relief is short-lived: by the end of stanza 4 the grief returns.

title: the fields of sleep
short: Unclear: perhaps the still-sleeping countryside at dawn, perhaps the west where the sun sets, perhaps the realm the soul came from.
body: Readers have proposed several meanings. Literally, the fields where people or flocks are still asleep in the early morning; or the quiet, distant uplands from which the wind comes; or, looking ahead to stanza 5 ('Our birth is but a sleep'), a mysterious region associated with the pre-existent life. The phrase is suggestive rather than precise, and the ambiguity is part of its effect.

title: a Tree, of many one, / A single Field
short: The turn: one particular tree and field, among many, remind him that something is lost.
body: 'Of many one' means one among many. The specificity is striking: not nature in general but a single tree and field 'speak of something that is gone'. Trilling stressed that the ode describes a change in perception that every adult experiences, not simply a failure of poetic power. The pansy continues the theme of particular objects bearing loss. Brooks emphasised the paradoxes of the ode's language; this passage turns the familiar Romantic delight in particular objects into a source of grief.

title: The Pansy
short: The pansy's name comes from French pensée, 'thought'; Ophelia's 'pansies, that's for thoughts' made the link proverbial.
body: Wordsworth's choice of flower brings with it its traditional meaning of thought or remembrance (Hamlet 4.5). The small flower 'doth the same tale repeat' of loss. It may be compared with the 'meanest flower that blows' of the last lines, where a flower again gives rise to thoughts, but now consoling ones. The flower is small and close at hand, 'at my feet', in contrast with the grand features of the May landscape, and it is the humble object rather than the grand one that speaks. This contrast between small and great objects runs through the poem.

anchor: Whither is fled the visionary gleam?
title: Whither is fled the visionary gleam?
short: The question that ends stanza 4, where Wordsworth broke off composition in 1802.
body: The two questions ('Whither ...? / Where is it now ...?') end the first movement. Wordsworth's later note told Isabella Fenwick that at least two years passed before he wrote the rest. Coleridge's 'Dejection' was in part an answer to the question. The rest of the ode offers two answers: a myth of pre-existence (stanzas 5-8) and a philosophical consolation (stanzas 9-11).

anchor: Our birth is but a sleep
title: Our birth is but a sleep and a forgetting
short: The myth of pre-existence: the soul existed before birth in a heavenly state and forgets it gradually.
body: In Plato's Phaedo and Meno, learning is recollection (anamnesis) of what the soul knew before birth; in the Republic's myth of Er souls drink from the river of forgetfulness before rebirth. Henry Vaughan's 'The Retreate' (1650) also looks back to an 'angel-infancy'. In the Fenwick note (1843) Wordsworth said he took up the notion of pre-existence as having enough foundation in human feeling to be used poetically, not as a doctrine he asserted. The inversion, birth as sleep, makes ordinary life a dream from which death might wake us.

title: trailing clouds of glory
short: The infant arrives still trailing the radiance of its divine origin.
body: 'Glory' in the biblical sense is the visible radiance of God's presence, often shown as cloud (e.g. Exodus 16:10, 'the glory of the LORD appeared in the cloud'). The children come 'not in utter nakedness': they carry something of heaven with them. The phrase has become one of the most quoted in English. The image of clouds trailing behind the newborn suggests both the light it brings and its gradual dispersal. It also connects with the closing stanza's clouds that 'gather round the setting sun' and take 'a sober colouring', so that the poem's arc runs from dawn clouds to sunset clouds.

title: Shades of the prison-house
short: The world, or the body, closing like a prison around the growing child.
body: The image of the body or this world as a prison is Platonic (Phaedo 62b, 82e) and was a commonplace of Christian devotion. 'Shades' means shadows, as the prison walls darken the light; there may also be a sense of 'ghosts'. The growing child still 'beholds the light'; the youth is 'Nature's Priest'; but the man sees it fade 'into the light of common day'. Critics note the inverted value: adulthood, ordinarily seen as growth, is pictured as imprisonment.

title: The Youth ... farther from the East ... Nature's Priest
short: The youth travels west like the sun, away from the dawn of his origin, yet still serves nature as priest.
body: The East is where the sun rises, and in Christian tradition the direction of Eden and of Christ's coming. The youth's journey west is the sun's course through the day toward evening. 'Nature's Priest' gives him a mediating, quasi-sacred role: he still ministers to the vision. Vaughan's 'The Retreate' similarly imagines the soul moving away from its first light. The structure of the stanza thus maps the ages of life onto the day: dawn, morning and the plain daylight of adulthood.

title: The homely Nurse ... her Foster-child, her Inmate Man
short: Earth is a well-meaning foster-mother who tries to make the child forget his royal origin.
body: 'Homely' means simple, domestic; 'inmate' an inhabitant, a lodger in someone else's house (not yet the modern sense of a prisoner, though it may be felt). The figure is of a royal child put out to nurse with a humble woman, a romance motif. 'That imperial palace whence he came' completes it. The stanza is notably gentle towards earth: her aim is 'no unworthy' one.

title: A four year's Darling of a pigmy size
short: The 1807 text; from 1815 Wordsworth read 'A six years' Darling'. The child is often identified with Hartley Coleridge.
body: Coleridge, quoting the ode in Biographia Literaria (1817), reads 'a six years' Darling of a pigmy size', showing the later reading; the archive preserves the earlier 'four year's'. Commentators have often connected the child with Hartley Coleridge (born 1796), to whom Wordsworth addressed 'To H. C., Six Years Old', though the poem does not name him. 'Fretted' here means touched and teased, not worried.

title: his "humourous stage"
short: Quoted from Samuel Daniel's dedicatory verses to Fulke Greville prefixed to Musophilus (1599).
body: The quotation marks signal a borrowing: Daniel's dedication opens 'I do not here upon this hum'rous stage'. 'Humorous' refers to the 'humours', the temperaments and moods of characters, as in comedies of humours. The child as 'little Actor' rehearsing roles recalls Jaques's 'All the world's a stage' in As You Like It (2.7), where life's ages run down to 'second childishness'; Wordsworth's 'palsied Age' sketches a similar sequence. 'Equipage' is a retinue or train of followers.

title: Thou best Philosopher ... Mighty Prophet! Seer blest!
short: The child is hailed as philosopher and prophet; Coleridge attacked the passage as 'mental bombast' in Biographia Literaria.
body: In chapter 22 of Biographia Literaria Coleridge cited this stanza as an example of 'thoughts and images too great for the subject'. He asked in what sense a child could be a philosopher or read 'the eternal deep', since the child is unconscious of these truths; such terms, he argued, would apply equally to a bee, a dog or a field of corn. Defenders reply that the child is 'Eye among the blind' because his way of being, not his thinking, embodies truths adults seek. 'Deaf and silent' is one of the obscurities Coleridge noted, since it is unclear whether it modifies 'Eye' or 'Philosopher'.

title: To whom the grave / Is but a lonely bed
short: Four lines that Wordsworth dropped from later editions; Coleridge criticised them in Biographia Literaria.
body: The child is said to imagine the grave as a bed where we lie awake, thinking, waiting. Coleridge objected that this made the passage only a comment on 'We are Seven', and protested at the frightful notion of lying awake in the grave, adding that Christian children learn to call death sleep. The lines did not appear in later collected editions; the archive's 1807 text preserves them.

title: obstinate questionings ... Fallings from us, vanishings
short: Wordsworth explained these as childhood moments when the outer world seemed unreal and he had to grasp a wall or tree to recall himself.
body: In the Fenwick note Wordsworth said that as a child he was often unable to think of external things as having external existence, and on the way to school would grasp at a wall or tree to recall himself 'from this abyss of idealism to the reality'. The 'blank misgivings of a Creature / Moving about in worlds not realiz'd' are these experiences, when the physical world seemed to fall away. The thanksgiving is for this sense of the mind's independence of sense, which he took as an intimation of immortality.

title: like a guilty Thing surpriz'd
short: Echoes Hamlet 1.1, where the Ghost 'started like a guilty thing / Upon a fearful summons' at cock-crow.
body: Horatio's lines describe the ghost fleeing the dawn. Wordsworth's 'mortal Nature' trembles before 'High instincts' as the ghost before day: the comparison reverses expectation by making our natural self the guilty spirit before a higher reality. The Shakespearean echo brings with it the supernatural atmosphere of the opening scene of Hamlet, where a ghost from another world must fade before the ordinary light of day. Wordsworth inverts the moral weight, since here it is the earthly self, not the visitant from another world, that is guilty and surprised.

title: that immortal sea / Which brought us hither
short: The sea of eternity from which souls come; in 'calm weather' the soul can glimpse it even far inland.
body: The seascape completes the myth: our origin is an ocean and we live 'inland far'. In moments of calm the soul can 'travel thither' and see 'the Children sport upon the shore', an image of the innocent beginning. Readers have noted that the children are seen from a distance, not rejoined. The sea image joins the poem's other waters: the cataracts of stanza 3, the 'fountain light' of stanza 9, and the 'Brooks which down their channels fret' in the last stanza.

title: years that bring the philosophic mind
short: The stanza's consolation: sympathy, suffering, faith and mature thought replace the lost radiance.
body: 'Primal sympathy' is the bond of feeling with nature and with others that existed from the beginning and 'must ever be'. The list of consolations ends in a 'philosophic mind', a reflective calm that, Trilling argued, is a real gain and not just a substitute. Critics differ on whether the consolation is convincing or a resigned acceptance of loss. The phrase recalls the classical ideal of philosophy as consolation (Boethius) and the Stoic acceptance of loss, but Wordsworth's version is grounded in feeling ('soothing thoughts that spring / Out of human suffering') rather than reason alone.

title: Another race hath been, and other palms are won
short: The race of life is run, and different prizes won: echoes St Paul's race and the palm of victory.
body: Paul compares the Christian life to a race in which one wins the prize (1 Corinthians 9:24), and in Revelation 7:9 the redeemed hold palms. The palm branch was the victor's token in ancient games. 'Another race' may also mean another generation. The line follows the 'sober colouring' given to the sunset by 'an eye / That hath kept watch o'er man's mortality', which revises the 'celestial light' of the opening.

title: the meanest flower that blows
short: 'Meanest' means humblest, most ordinary; 'blows' means blooms.
body: In the older sense 'mean' is lowly, common; 'blow' (Old English blowan) means to bloom, a verb distinct from 'blow' of wind. The last lines give the consolation its final form: the mature heart, through its tenderness, joys and fears, finds in the humblest flower thoughts that are beyond weeping. Compare the pansy of stanza 4, which spoke only of loss.
